paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds representations from unlabeled data, but understanding its success requires accounting for the transformations applied to training examples. This paper focuses on a gap in existing theory: data augmentation is often treated too generally to explain how particular augmentation choices affect what a model learns.

The authors derive an error bound that explicitly includes augmentation. It connects supervised risk, which concerns performance on a labeled task, to both the unsupervised training risk and a trade-off introduced by augmentation. This means the theoretical account cannot assess downstream performance solely from how well the contrastive objective is optimized; the augmentation contribution also enters the bound.

Under a proposed semantic label assumption, the paper examines how certain augmentation methods change that bound. The authors then test their theoretical results with experiments at both the pixel and representation levels. The contribution is a way to reason about augmentation as part of the learning mechanism, with the analysis of specific methods depending on the stated semantic assumption.
icml-2025-an-augmentation-aware-theory-f.tldr: An augmentation-aware error bound connects contrastive learning performance to an explicit trade-off introduced by data augmentation.

paragraphs: Autoregressive and recurrent networks can make strong predictions while offering insufficient guidance about their uncertainty. That gap matters in scientific applications, where a useful model must support judgments about how much to trust its output. BARNN introduces a variational Bayesian framework intended to give these sequence models a principled treatment of uncertainty.

The approach builds on variational dropout, making it applicable to large recurrent networks as well. It also introduces a temporal version of the Variational Mixtures of Posteriors prior, called tVAMP-prior. Together, these components are designed to make Bayesian inference efficient and well calibrated, while supporting the broader aim of converting autoregressive or recurrent models into Bayesian versions.

Experiments cover partial differential equation modeling and molecular generation. In those settings, the authors report accuracy comparable to or better than existing methods, alongside strong uncertainty quantification and modeling of long-range dependencies. The results suggest that adding an explicit uncertainty framework can coexist with competitive predictive performance in the scientific tasks studied.
icml-2025-barnn-a-bayesian-autoregressiv.tldr: BARNN adds variational Bayesian uncertainty modeling to autoregressive and recurrent networks, with promising results on PDE modeling and molecular generation.

paragraphs: Predicting video watch time requires handling more than a single smooth pattern of viewing behavior. The authors observe that, among videos in the same duration bucket, watch ratio can have several distinct peaks. They argue that existing label transformations overlook this distribution and can leave individual example representations insufficiently distinguished.

ProWTP addresses these issues in two stages. A hierarchical vector quantised variational autoencoder converts the continuous label distribution into a high-dimensional discrete representation, providing prototypes for calibration. The method then aligns example representations with these prototypes through a semi-relaxed unbalanced optimal transport problem, allowing flexibility in the constraints assigned to prototypes.

The authors reformulate that alignment problem as weighted Lasso for its solution. Additional assignment and compactness losses encourage examples to gather around their corresponding prototypes, making the groups easier to distinguish. ProWTP is presented as compatible with any deep recommendation model. Offline experiments on two industrial datasets report consistent improvements, supporting the value of explicitly modeling watch-ratio structure and aligning representations with it.
icml-2025-calibrating-video-watch-time-p.tldr: ProWTP improves watch-time prediction by learning prototypes of watch-ratio patterns and aligning example representations with them.

paragraphs: Causal abstraction connects detailed descriptions of a system to higher-level descriptions. This paper studies learning that connection in a difficult setting: the structural causal models are inaccessible, intervention data is unavailable, and samples at the two levels are not aligned. The task is therefore to learn from distributions without directly matching individual observations.

The central assumption is semantic embedding: the high-level distribution lies within a subspace of the low-level distribution. The authors use a category-theoretic formulation to express abstraction learning as finding a mapping between probability measures that respects this principle. For linear abstractions, the principle connects the problem to the geometry of the Stiefel manifold.

The paper develops a concrete solution for linear causal abstraction with Gaussian measures, using Kullback–Leibler divergence as the objective. Because the optimization is nonconvex, it proposes three algorithms based on Riemannian optimization. Tests on synthetic data and real brain data report success with varying amounts of prior structural information, supporting the framework within the modeled setting.
icml-2025-causal-abstraction-learning-ba.tldr: A semantic embedding principle enables causal abstraction learning from unaligned distributions, with algorithms for linear Gaussian abstractions.

paragraphs: Clinical AI benchmarks often cover only a small collection of data types and tasks. CLIMB expands that scope by bringing together imaging, language, temporal, and graph modalities in one benchmark. Its purpose is to support research on models that can combine diverse clinical information when assessing patient health.

The benchmark contains 4.51 million patient samples and 19.01 terabytes of data, spanning 2D imaging, 3D video, time series, graphs, and multimodal data. The authors use it to investigate multitask pretraining and report improvements over single-task learning of up to 29% for ultrasound and 23% for ECG analysis. These are reported gains in the evaluated settings, rather than uniform improvements across every task.

The experiments also find that CLIMB pretraining improves generalization to new tasks. Strong encoders for individual modalities translate well to multimodal performance when paired with fusion strategies suited to the task. Together, the findings connect broader training data with decisions about encoder quality and how different information sources should be combined.
icml-2025-climb-data-foundations-for-lar.tldr: CLIMB unifies diverse clinical data and demonstrates benefits from multitask pretraining and task-appropriate multimodal fusion.

paragraphs: Local gradient descent lets clients perform multiple updates between communication rounds. Existing analyses for heterogeneous objectives restrict the stepsize to at most 1/K, where K is the communication interval, to keep the objective decreasing monotonically. This paper examines whether that restriction is needed for logistic regression with separable, heterogeneous data.

The authors allow any positive constant stepsize η. They show that, after an initial unstable phase, convergence follows a rate of O(1/(ηKR)), where R is the number of communication rounds. The initial phase lasts roughly O(ηKM) rounds, up to the factors suppressed by the stated bound, with M denoting the number of clients.

The result exposes a trade-off: larger stepsizes or longer local update intervals improve the eventual rate while lengthening the bound on the unstable phase. The analysis improves on the cited O(1/R) rate for general smooth convex objectives in this specific setting. It also identifies heterogeneous local updates as a source of instability, alongside extremely large stepsizes.
icml-2025-constant-stepsize-local-gd-for.tldr: For separable heterogeneous logistic regression, Local GD can converge faster after an unstable phase without restricting the positive constant stepsize.

paragraphs: Continual generalized category discovery asks a model to learn new categories from an unlabeled stream while retaining previously learned categories. The challenge intensifies when the stream mixes familiar and unfamiliar classes. This paper analyzes forgetting from a Bayesian perspective and identifies covariance misalignment between old and new classes as a driver of declining performance.

The proposed VB-CGCD framework combines variational inference with a nearest-class-mean classifier that accounts for covariance. Rather than relying only on class centers, the method incorporates how class distributions vary. It adaptively aligns those distributions and uses stochastic variational updates to suppress noise from pseudo-labels, the labels assigned by the model itself.

On standard benchmarks, the authors report a +15.21% improvement over prior art in final-session overall accuracy. They also introduce a harder benchmark with only 10% labeled data and longer online phases. There, VB-CGCD reaches 67.86% final accuracy compared with 38.55% for the stated state of the art. These results support distribution alignment as a useful approach to learning new categories while reducing forgetting.
icml-2025-continual-generalized-category.tldr: VB-CGCD uses Bayesian distribution alignment to reduce forgetting and pseudo-label noise during continual discovery of new categories.

paragraphs: A randomized controlled trial can spend substantial resources testing treatments that have little impact. This paper asks how to allocate a trial so that it can certify a strong effect for at least one treatment. Its objective is specifically to obtain a high-probability lower bound on the best-performing treatment effect.

The proposed design has two stages. First, a data-driven screening procedure removes low-impact treatments. Second, the trial focuses on establishing lower bounds for the strongest remaining treatment effect. The authors derive optimal designs for this two-stage formulation and show how to implement them through sample splitting. This structure is intended for settings where repeatedly adapting a trial is difficult.

Empirical results favor the two-stage designs over single-stage approaches, especially when prior knowledge about the treatments is available. The significance is that screening can improve how trial resources support a treatment-effect guarantee. The claimed benefit concerns the strength of a probabilistic certificate for at least one studied arm, rather than a promise that every treatment will be well estimated.
icml-2025-data-driven-design-of-randomiz.tldr: A two-stage trial screens out weak treatments before concentrating resources on certifying a strong treatment effect with high probability.

paragraphs: Maintaining a private count of distinct items becomes difficult when a dataset changes through both additions and deletions and results must be released continually. The stream and the universe of possible items may both be enormous. This paper develops algorithms that reduce memory requirements while preserving differential privacy in this turnstile setting.

For arbitrary streams of length T, the algorithm uses Oη(T^(1/3)) space and additive error, together with a multiplicative approximation factor of 1+η for any η between zero and one. This replaces prior linear memory requirements with sublinear space. Its additive error approaches, but does not match, the known Ω(T^(1/4)) lower bound for arbitrary streams.

When a bound W on how often an item appears is known, both memory and additive error become Oη(√W). That error asymptotically matches earlier results that needed linear space. The paper also proves an Ω(T^(1/3)) memory lower bound for algorithms using similar techniques, identifying a boundary for this approach rather than for every possible algorithm.
icml-2025-differentially-private-space-e.tldr: New differentially private algorithms count distinct items under additions and deletions using sublinear memory with quantified approximation error.

paragraphs: An edge-colored hypergraph represents objects participating in different types of group interactions. Clustering assigns a color to each object, and an interaction is satisfied only when all its objects match its color. This paper extends the usual goal of minimizing unsatisfied interactions to other objectives that capture different priorities.

The first extension maximizes satisfied interactions. Although maximizing successes and minimizing failures have the same optimal solutions here, their approximation guarantees behave differently. The authors provide the first approximation algorithm for the maximization problem on hypergraphs, where interactions can involve more than two objects. They then refine the method to improve the best-known approximation factor for ordinary graphs.

The paper also introduces objectives incorporating balance and fairness. For these formulations, it establishes hardness results, approximation algorithms, and fixed-parameter tractability results. These contributions explain both what can be computed efficiently and where difficulty remains. The broader message is that choosing an objective changes the available algorithmic guarantees, even when two objectives agree on the ideal solution.
icml-2025-edge-colored-clustering-in-hyp.tldr: The paper develops approximation algorithms for satisfied-edge maximization and studies balance and fairness in edge-colored hypergraph clustering.

paragraphs: Prompt learning can adapt a large vision-language model to a particular target, yet that adaptation may transfer poorly to other tasks or settings. The authors suggest that overfitting during training may cause the model to forget general knowledge. Their Features Matrix approach aims to preserve and use that knowledge when broader generalization matters.

The Features Matrix extracts semantic information from diverse inputs at a deep and fine-grained level. It is designed to retain useful general knowledge and reduce the risk of overfitting during adaptation. The authors present it as a generic module that can fit within existing frameworks, making preservation of general information part of the adaptation process.

Evaluations examine generalization from base to novel categories, across domains, and across datasets. The paper reports compatibility with existing frameworks and state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated generalization tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the Features Matrix in those settings. The explanation that forgetting causes prompting difficulties remains a proposed motivation, rather than an established universal account of why transfer fails.
icml-2025-enhancing-target-unspecific-ta.tldr: A Features Matrix preserves general semantic knowledge to improve vision-language model generalization beyond the targets used for adaptation.

paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference combines experimental data with machine learning predictions to support valid statistical conclusions. When enough high-quality predictions are available, it can improve estimation accuracy and tighten confidence intervals. FAB-PPI extends this framework by incorporating prior knowledge about how good those predictions are expected to be.

The method uses Bayesian information to assist a procedure that retains frequentist guarantees. Its improvement over standard PPI is conditional: it occurs when the observed prediction quality is plausible under the prior. The prior therefore supplies useful information when its expectations agree with the observed evidence, without replacing the method’s frequentist validity guarantees.

The paper also describes a protective adaptation obtained with heavy-tailed priors. In regions assigned low prior probability, FAB-PPI moves back toward standard PPI. This behavior matters when actual prediction quality differs from prior expectations, because the method can reduce its reliance on that prior. Real and synthetic examples demonstrate benefits, supporting a way to use prior knowledge while retaining the underlying statistical guarantees.
icml-2025-fab-ppi-frequentist-assisted-b.tldr: FAB-PPI uses prior knowledge about prediction quality to improve inference when that knowledge fits the data while retaining frequentist guarantees.

paragraphs: Domain randomization trains a robot across varied simulated environments so that its controller can tolerate uncertainty in the properties being randomized. Usually, someone chooses the training distribution by hand. This paper instead learns that distribution, making the choice of simulated conditions part of the learning problem.

The authors represent the sampling distribution with a normalizing flow and optimize it through entropy-regularized reward maximization. This gives the distribution more flexibility than the simple parameterized distributions used by existing approaches. The paper reports that the added flexibility produces better robustness, and demonstrates robust policies for assembly tasks involving substantial physical contact.

The work also considers how individually learned skills can support a multi-step manipulation planner. It explores combining the learned sampling distributions with a privileged value function to detect conditions outside the training distribution. This connects training-time environment selection with uncertainty awareness during planning. The planning component is presented as an exploration of this use, while the stated robustness gains concern the learned policies and evaluated comparisons.
icml-2025-flow-based-domain-randomizatio.tldr: Learning simulation distributions with normalizing flows improves robotic policy robustness and supports exploration of uncertainty-aware skill sequencing.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds for an iterative learning algorithm can become less useful if they keep growing with the number of training steps. This paper establishes bounds for Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics that remain finite independently of iteration count. The analysis covers smooth nonconvex losses in unbounded settings.

The proof studies stability by comparing two learning sequences run on datasets sampled from the same distribution. Under an isoperimetric inequality restricting the loss tails, the authors keep the sequences within bounded Kullback–Leibler divergence. This relaxes assumptions used in previous work and shows that strong convexity is not necessary for finite stability bounds.

An additional dissipativity assumption allows the authors to bound the stronger Rényi divergence by establishing a uniform log-Sobolev constant for the iterates. Without dissipativity, they instead use the regularizing effect of Gaussian convolution. These two routes clarify which assumptions support which conclusions. Overall, the work establishes that noisy gradient methods can have iteration-independent generalization and differential privacy bounds under the conditions analyzed.
icml-2025-generalization-of-noisy-sgd-in.tldr: The paper proves iteration-independent generalization and privacy bounds for noisy gradient methods under assumptions allowing unbounded nonconvex settings.

paragraphs: Many classifiers treat the concepts represented by their classes as precisely defined. This paper takes inspiration from the cognitive-science view that real-world concepts are often ambiguous. Its Human Cognition-Inspired Hierarchical Fuzzy Learning Machine aims to incorporate human class knowledge into learning while accommodating that ambiguity.

The central mechanism is a hierarchical alignment loss. It brings the hierarchical structure learned from data into correspondence with the structure represented in class knowledge. The authors theoretically prove that minimizing this loss can produce such alignment. This gives the learned hierarchy an explicit semantic connection to the supplied knowledge, supporting interpretation of what the model has learned.

Systematic experiments report significant improvements in both interpretability and generalization. The approach therefore links its training objective, theoretical result, and empirical findings around one idea: relationships among concepts should help organize the classifier’s learned structure. Its significance lies in using class knowledge within the learning process itself, so that predictive learning and semantic organization can support one another.
icml-2025-human-cognition-inspired-hiera.tldr: HC-HFLM uses a hierarchical alignment loss to connect learned class structure with human knowledge, improving interpretability and generalization in experiments.

paragraphs: Neural Theorem Provers combine differentiable learning with interpretable symbolic logic, but their optimization can be difficult because the objective landscape is complex and gradients are sparse. Knowledge graph embedding methods offer smoother optimization with clear learning objectives, although they often provide less interpretability. This paper investigates ways to combine their strengths.

One strategy uses the structural learning capabilities of knowledge graph embeddings to improve the embedding space of a Neural Theorem Prover. This addresses how the prover’s learned representations are organized, targeting an obstacle to effective optimization. Across the proposed integration strategies, the authors report substantial improvements in accuracy and computational efficiency.

Another strategy replaces Neural Theorem Prover computations with efficient knowledge graph embedding operations. On a large-scale dataset such as WN18RR, the paper reports evaluation speedups exceeding 1000 times, with a mild accuracy trade-off. That qualification matters: the fastest substitution does not promise simultaneous accuracy gains. The contribution offers ways to improve representation learning and ways to exchange a small accuracy loss for much faster evaluation.
icml-2025-improving-soft-unification-wit.tldr: Knowledge graph embedding techniques improve Neural Theorem Prover representations and enable much faster evaluation with a mild accuracy trade-off.

paragraphs: Inferring gene regulatory networks from expression data aims to uncover how genes regulate one another. Supervised methods depend on expensive ground-truth labels and may learn gene-specific labeling biases instead of regulatory mechanisms. InfoSEM addresses both concerns with an unsupervised generative model informed by textual representations of genes.

The model uses textual gene embeddings as informative priors, allowing it to infer networks without ground-truth interaction labels. When labels are available, it can incorporate them as another prior; the authors present this as a way to improve performance while avoiding the identified biases. They also introduce a biologically motivated benchmark designed to reflect applications such as biomarker discovery and expose biases learned by supervised methods.

Across four datasets, InfoSEM reports a 38.5% improvement over existing models when using textual embedding priors, followed by a further 11.1% improvement when labeled data is added as prior information. These findings support using biological knowledge through priors and evaluating whether apparent predictive success reflects useful regulatory information rather than label patterns.
icml-2025-infosem-a-deep-generative-mode.tldr: InfoSEM uses textual gene embeddings as priors for unsupervised regulatory network inference and introduces benchmarking aimed at revealing label biases.

paragraphs: Safety alignment helps language models resist harmful instructions, but it can also cause them to reject harmless requests. ACTOR targets this over-refusal problem by examining the model’s internal activation patterns. The aim is to reduce unnecessary refusals while preserving the model’s ability to respond appropriately to harmful queries.

The framework uses activations from diverse queries to identify and adjust components that trigger refusal. It fine-tunes only a single model layer, focusing the training intervention on internal representations associated with that behavior. The authors describe this approach as efficient in both computation and data, with stronger control over the refusal mechanism.

Across multiple benchmarks, ACTOR reduces over-refusals while maintaining harmful-query handling and overall utility. The significance is the combination of these outcomes: more responses to benign prompts would be less useful if the model also lost its safety behavior or general capabilities. The reported evaluations support targeted representation adjustment as a way to improve that balance, with a narrowly scoped fine-tuning intervention.
icml-2025-just-enough-shifts-mitigating-.tldr: ACTOR fine-tunes refusal-related activations in one model layer to reduce benign refusals while preserving safety handling and utility in evaluations.

paragraphs: Different heuristics for an online problem may work well on different kinds of inputs. This paper studies how to compete with the best available heuristic for a Metrical Task System when only one heuristic’s action can be queried at each time step. The algorithm must choose what to consult while processing the incoming instance.

The main obstacle is that observing a heuristic once does not reveal enough to estimate its current cost. That estimate also requires having queried the same heuristic at the preceding step. Switching which heuristic is observed therefore affects the information available for comparison. The authors connect this difficulty to bandit learning against adversaries with bounded memory.

The paper gives an algorithm achieving regret of O(OPT^(2/3)) and proves a matching lower bound. Together, these results establish a tight regret scale for the studied setting. The contribution explains both how to combine specialized heuristics under restricted access and why the dependence between consecutive observations imposes an unavoidable performance barrier.
icml-2025-learning-augmented-algorithms-.tldr: The paper establishes tight regret bounds for combining Metrical Task System heuristics when only one predictor can be queried per step.

paragraphs: A graph-learning benchmark should help reveal what graph-learning methods can do. Yet some datasets allow methods that ignore graph structure to outperform graph-based approaches. This paper shifts attention from evaluating models to evaluating the datasets used to judge them, asking what makes a benchmark informative for graph learning.

The proposed RINGS framework examines the two information sources in these datasets: graph structure and node features. It perturbs these modes and compares the altered datasets with the originals. These dataset ablations provide a way to investigate the role of each information source rather than relying only on model scores from the unchanged dataset.

Within this framework, the authors introduce performance separability and mode complementarity as two distinct evaluation measures. Each assesses a different aspect of a dataset’s ability to benchmark graph-learning methods. Experiments on graph-level tasks demonstrate the framework’s usefulness and lead to recommendations for evaluation practice. The contribution is a flexible method for scrutinizing benchmarks themselves, recognizing that dataset quality has more than one relevant dimension.
icml-2025-no-metric-to-rule-them-all-tow.tldr: RINGS evaluates graph-learning datasets by perturbing graph structure and node features and measuring distinct aspects of benchmark quality.

paragraphs: A classifier can express confidence through calibrated probabilities or through a set of plausible labels. Conformal prediction constructs such sets with a specified marginal coverage guarantee, but that guarantee does not ensure the same coverage for every class. This paper studies how temperature scaling, a common calibration method, interacts with conformal prediction.

An extensive empirical study finds that temperature scaling improves class-conditional coverage for adaptive conformal methods while making prediction set sizes worse. The result exposes a tension between two desirable properties: more even coverage across classes and smaller, more informative candidate sets. Better probability calibration therefore does not automatically improve every aspect of the resulting prediction sets.

The authors then investigate temperature scaling beyond its usual calibration purpose. They identify a non-monotonic relationship that allows trading set size against conditional coverage, and develop mathematical theory explaining the full trend. Based on the theory and experiments, they offer practical guidance for combining calibration with adaptive conformal prediction according to the user’s priorities.
icml-2025-on-temperature-scaling-and-con.tldr: Temperature scaling creates a theoretically explained trade-off between prediction set size and class-conditional coverage in adaptive conformal prediction.

paragraphs: A language model can become less helpful when safety training leads it to reject harmless requests. Measuring this over-refusal systematically is difficult because researchers need benign prompts that actually provoke unnecessary refusals. This paper introduces an automatic method for producing such prompts at scale and uses it to build OR-Bench.

The benchmark contains 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 common rejection categories. It also includes roughly 1,000 particularly difficult prompts that challenge even leading models. An additional set of 600 toxic prompts checks the opposite concern: a system should not appear better simply because it responds indiscriminately to both benign and harmful requests.

The authors use OR-Bench to study 32 language models across eight model families, providing a broad evaluation of over-refusal behavior. They release the datasets and code publicly. The contribution is a repeatable way to examine whether safety-aligned models remain useful on innocuous requests while retaining a check on harmful responses, making this balance easier to evaluate during model development.
icml-2025-or-bench-an-over-refusal-bench.tldr: OR-Bench measures unnecessary language-model refusals with automatically generated benign prompts and a complementary set of harmful prompts.

paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference uses machine learning predictions to help make statistical conclusions when directly obtained data is scarce or costly. Existing approaches largely focus on Z-estimation problems, including means and quantiles. This paper extends the idea to e-values, opening a broader route for incorporating predictions into statistical procedures.

The central result is that every inference procedure expressible through e-values has a prediction-powered counterpart under the proposed method. This preserves the usual benefits of e-values, including anytime validity, post-hoc validity, and flexible sequential inference. The scope is broad but specific: the result applies to procedures that can be framed in terms of e-values.

The authors demonstrate the framework on hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, change-point detection, and causal discovery. The latter tasks extend beyond what the previous techniques described in the abstract could handle. Because the approach is modular, it can be integrated into existing algorithms. Its significance is the expansion of prediction-powered inference from a relatively narrow set of estimation tasks to a general family of evidence-based procedures.
icml-2025-prediction-powered-e-values-a2.tldr: The framework gives e-value-based inference procedures prediction-powered counterparts while retaining their sequential and validity benefits.

paragraphs: This paper applies self-play to autonomous driving, training a policy entirely through interactions in simulation rather than human driving data. The authors report that robust and naturalistic behavior emerges after 1.6 billion kilometers of simulated driving. The work examines whether self-play can succeed beyond the game settings where it has been especially influential.

The training scale is enabled by Gigaflow, a batched simulator that can generate and train on 42 years of subjective driving experience per hour using a single node with eight GPUs. The resulting policy achieves state-of-the-art performance on three independent driving benchmarks. It also exceeds the prior state of the art in evaluations using recorded real-world scenarios amid human drivers.

The authors find that the policy behaves realistically when compared with human references, despite never seeing human data during training. In simulation, it averages 17.5 years of continuous driving between incidents. That robustness figure describes simulated performance. Together, the findings support large-scale simulated self-play as a source of driving behavior that performs well in the reported evaluations.
icml-2025-robust-autonomy-emerges-from-s.tldr: Large-scale simulated self-play produces a driving policy with strong benchmark performance and realistic behavior without human training data.

paragraphs: Removing unwanted concepts from a text-to-image diffusion model can be difficult to interpret: a method may change behavior without making the internal intervention clear. SAeUron addresses this by using sparse autoencoders to identify interpretable features associated with particular concepts and then intervening on those features.

The autoencoders are trained without supervision on model activations collected across multiple denoising timesteps. The authors show that they capture sparse features corresponding to specific concepts. A feature selection method then targets model activations to block unwanted content while preserving overall performance. This connects the removal procedure to identifiable internal representations.

SAeUron outperforms existing approaches on UnlearnCanvas for concept and style unlearning, and the authors report effective elimination of nudity in the I2P evaluation. A single sparse autoencoder can also support removal of multiple concepts simultaneously. Under adversarial attack, the method reduces the possibility of generating unwanted content compared with other methods. That result supports improved resistance in the evaluated attacks, rather than a universal guarantee that targeted content can never reappear.
icml-2025-saeuron-interpretable-concept-.tldr: SAeUron uses interpretable sparse-autoencoder features to remove unwanted diffusion-model concepts while preserving performance and improving resistance to evaluated attacks.
